items.title: Governors-General of Bengal (1773-1833): Hastings to Wellesley
items.body:
## From Company official to Governor-General

- **Warren Hastings (1772-1785)** — became Governor of Bengal in 1772 and the **first Governor-General of Bengal** under the **Regulating Act of 1773**. Established the **Supreme Court at Fort William (1774)** and founded the **Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784)** with William Jones. **Pitt's India Act (1784)** was passed in his tenure; he was later impeached in England over the Chait Singh affair.
- **Lord Cornwallis (1786-1793)** — the **'Father of Civil Services in India'**; introduced the **Permanent Settlement (1793)**, set up appellate and lower courts, and signed the **Treaty of Seringapatam** (Third Anglo-Mysore War).
- **Sir John Shore (1793-1798)** — Charter Act of 1793; policy of **non-intervention**.
- **Lord Wellesley (1798-1805)** — introduced the **Subsidiary Alliance System**, signed the **Treaty of Bassein**, fought the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, and founded **Fort William College (1800)**.

## Constitutional Acts linkage

| Act | Year | Tenure |
|---|---|---|
| Regulating Act | 1773 | Warren Hastings |
| Pitt's India Act | 1784 | Warren Hastings |
| Charter Act | 1793 | John Shore |
| Charter Act | 1813 | Lord Minto I |
| Charter Act | 1833 | Lord William Bentinck |
keyPoints: Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal (Regulating Act 1773) and founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784).
Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement (1793) and is called the Father of Civil Services in India.
Lord Wellesley introduced the Subsidiary Alliance system and founded Fort William College (1800).
Pitt's India Act (1784) was passed during Warren Hastings' tenure.
The Charter Act of 1813 fell under Lord Minto I and the Charter Act of 1833 under Lord William Bentinck.
items.mnemonic: Bengal GG order: 'Hastings Cornwallis Shore Wellesley' — H-C-S-W.

items.title: Reforming Governors-General: Bentinck & Dalhousie
items.body:
## Lord William Bentinck (1828-1835)

- The most **liberal and enlightened** Governor-General; **abolished Sati (1829)** and suppressed **Thuggee**, infanticide and child sacrifice.
- Became the **first Governor-General of India** under the **Charter Act of 1833**, which barred debarring any Indian from office on grounds of religion, birth, descent or colour.
- **Father of modern Western education in India** — backed the **English Education Act (1835)** and established the Medical College, Kolkata.

## Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856)

- The great **moderniser**: opened the first **railway line (Bombay-Thane, 1853)**, laid ~4000 miles of **telegraph** lines, and brought the **Post Office Act (1854)**.
- Introduced the **Doctrine of Lapse** to annex states (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, etc.).
- Implemented **Wood's Dispatch (1854)** — the 'Magna Carta of English education in India'.
- Fought the Second Anglo-Sikh War and set up separate Public Works Departments.
keyPoints: Lord William Bentinck abolished Sati in 1829 and became the first Governor-General of India under the Charter Act of 1833.
Bentinck backed the English Education Act (1835) and is called the Father of modern Western education in India.
Lord Dalhousie opened the first railway line (Bombay-Thane) in 1853 and introduced the Doctrine of Lapse.
Dalhousie implemented Wood's Dispatch (1854) and laid the telegraph and postal systems.
Wood's Dispatch (1854) is called the Magna Carta of English education in India.
items.mnemonic: Dalhousie = 'Doctrine + Development' — Doctrine of Lapse plus railways, telegraph, post.

items.title: Lord Canning & the Transition to Crown Rule (1858)
items.body:
## Lord Canning (1856-1862)

- Served as **Governor-General until 1858** and then as the **first Viceroy of India** — the office spanning the transition.
- Oversaw the **Revolt of 1857**.
- Established the **universities at Calcutta, Madras and Bombay (1857)**.

## Government of India Act 1858

- Passed as an 'Act of Good Governance': it **abolished the East India Company** and transferred power to the **British Crown**.
- Followed by the **Queen's Proclamation** of 1858 and army reorganisation.
- The **Indian Councils Act 1861** introduced the portfolio system and the beginnings of legislative devolution.

> After 1858 the head of the Indian administration held the dual title of **Governor-General and Viceroy**.
keyPoints: Lord Canning was the last Governor-General and the first Viceroy of India.
The Government of India Act 1858 abolished the East India Company and transferred power to the British Crown.
Canning established the universities of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay in 1857.
The Indian Councils Act 1861 introduced the portfolio (budget) system.
The Revolt of 1857 unfolded during Canning's tenure and triggered Crown rule.
items.mnemonic: Canning 'closes the Company' — GoI Act 1858 ends EIC rule.

items.title: Early Viceroys: Mayo, Lytton, Ripon & Dufferin
items.body:
## Key early Viceroys (1869-1888)

| Viceroy | Tenure | Landmark associations |
|---|---|---|
| **Lord Mayo** | 1869-1872 | Financial **decentralisation**; first regular **Census (1872)**; Mayo College; assassinated at Port Blair |
| **Lord Lytton** | 1876-1880 | **Vernacular Press Act** & **Arms Act**; Durbar proclaiming **Queen Victoria as Empress (1877)**; abolished cotton tax |
| **Lord Ripon** | 1880-1884 | **Repealed** the Vernacular Press Act; **local self-government** ('Father of Local Self-Government'); **Ilbert Bill**; Hunter Commission |
| **Lord Dufferin** | 1884-1888 | Founding of the **Indian National Congress (1885)**; Third Anglo-Burmese War |

- **Contrast to remember:** Lytton *imposed* the Vernacular Press Act (1878); Ripon *repealed* it (1882).
- The **Ilbert Bill** controversy (allowing Indian judges to try Europeans) energised early nationalist politics.
keyPoints: Lord Mayo introduced financial decentralisation and conducted the first Census (1872); he was assassinated at Port Blair.
Lord Lytton passed the Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act and proclaimed Queen Victoria Empress of India (1877).
Lord Ripon repealed the Vernacular Press Act and is the Father of Local Self-Government; he introduced the Ilbert Bill.
The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 during Lord Dufferin's viceroyalty.
Lytton imposed the Vernacular Press Act (1878); Ripon repealed it (1882).
items.mnemonic: Press seesaw: Lytton locks the press, Ripon releases it.

items.title: Curzon, Minto II & Hardinge II: Partition Politics
items.body:
## Lord Curzon (1899-1905)

- Introduced the **Indian Universities Act** and **partitioned Bengal (1905)** — a spark for the Swadeshi Movement.
- Strengthened **archaeology/conservation** (Archaeological Survey of India); appointed the Raleigh Commission; embroiled in the Curzon-Kitchener controversy.

## Lord Minto II (1905-1910)

- Enacted the **Morley-Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909)** introducing **separate electorates**.
- His period saw the founding of the **Muslim League (1906)** and the Swadeshi agitation.

## Lord Hardinge II (1910-1916)

- **Annulled the Partition of Bengal** and **transferred the capital from Calcutta to Delhi** (announced at the 1911 Delhi Durbar).
- The Hindu Mahasabha was established during his tenure.
keyPoints: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905 and introduced the Indian Universities Act.
The Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) introducing separate electorates came under Lord Minto II.
The Muslim League was founded in 1906 during Minto II's tenure.
Lord Hardinge II annulled the Bengal partition and shifted the capital to Delhi (announced 1911).
Curzon's tenure strengthened the Archaeological Survey of India.
items.mnemonic: Curzon cuts Bengal (1905); Hardinge heals it (1911) and moves to Delhi.

items.title: Late Viceroys: Chelmsford to Mountbatten
items.body:
## Towards Independence (1916-1948)

| Viceroy | Tenure | Landmark associations |
|---|---|---|
| **Lord Chelmsford** | 1916-1921 | **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919)** (dyarchy); **Rowlatt Act**; **Jallianwala Bagh (1919)** |
| **Lord Reading** | 1921-1926 | Chauri Chaura incident; Swaraj Party |
| **Lord Irwin** | 1926-1931 | **Civil Disobedience** & **Dandi March (1930)**; First Round Table Conference; **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)** |
| **Lord Willingdon** | 1931-1936 | Second & Third RTCs; **Communal Award** & **Poona Pact (1932)** |
| **Lord Linlithgow** | 1936-1944 | **Cripps Mission**; **Quit India Movement (1942)** |
| **Lord Wavell** | 1944-1947 | **CR Formula**; **Shimla Conference**; **Direct Action Day (1946)** |
| **Lord Mountbatten** | 1947-1948 | **June 3rd Plan**; **last Viceroy** & **first Governor-General of free India** |

- Note the succession: **Wavell** proposed the CR Formula and held Shimla (1945); **Mountbatten** brought the partition plan and transfer of power.
keyPoints: Lord Chelmsford's tenure saw the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (1919), the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh.
Lord Irwin saw the Civil Disobedience Movement, the Dandi March (1930) and the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931).
Lord Linlithgow managed the Cripps Mission and the Quit India Movement (1942).
Lord Wavell introduced the CR Formula, organised the Shimla Conference and saw Direct Action Day (1946).
Lord Mountbatten proposed the June 3rd Plan and was the last Viceroy and first Governor-General of independent India.
items.mnemonic: Last five Viceroys: 'Chelmsford Reading Irwin Willingdon Linlithgow ... Wavell Mountbatten'.

items.title: Land Settlements, Educational Institutions & Committees (PYQ set)
items.body:
## Three land-revenue settlements

| Settlement | Author(s) | Region | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Permanent / Zamindari** (1793) | **Cornwallis** (with John Shore) | Bengal, Bihar, Orissa | Zamindar = owner; fixed revenue forever |
| **Ryotwari** | **Alexander Read & Thomas Munro** | Madras & Bombay | Revenue settled directly with the ryot (cultivator) |
| **Mahalwari** | **Holt Mackenzie & R.M. Bird** (Regulation 1822/1833) | North-West Provinces, Punjab | Revenue settled with the village/mahal |

## Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley, 1798) — key features

- Ally kept a British force and paid for it (cede territory instead of cash); a British Resident at court; no other alliances or wars without British consent; British defended the ally. It did **not** aim to secure a fixed income for the Company (a common exam trap).
- **Fort William College (1800)** was founded by Wellesley **to train newly-arrived British civil servants** in Indian languages and administration.

## Educational institutions & their founders

- **Calcutta Madarsa (1781)** — **Warren Hastings** (Islamic law/Arabic-Persian studies).
- **Sanskrit College, Benaras (1791)** — **Jonathan Duncan**.
- **Fort William College (1800)** — **Wellesley**.

## Committees to remember

- **Butler Committee (1927)** — examined the relationship between the **Government of India (Crown) and the Indian princely states** (paramountcy).
- **Hunter Commission (1882)** — education, under Ripon; **Wood's Dispatch (1854)** — grants-in-aid, universities, under Dalhousie.
keyPoints: Permanent Settlement (1793, Cornwallis) — Bengal; Ryotwari (Read & Munro) — Madras/Bombay; Mahalwari (Holt Mackenzie & R.M. Bird) — NW Provinces.
Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley 1798) did NOT aim to secure a fixed income for the Company — it was about troops, a Resident and no independent alliances.
Fort William College (1800, Wellesley) trained British civil servants for administration.
Calcutta Madarsa (1781) = Warren Hastings; Sanskrit College Benaras (1791) = Jonathan Duncan.
Butler Committee (1927) examined Government of India–princely states (paramountcy) relations.
items.mnemonic: Land settlements RPM: Ryotwari (Read/Munro), Permanent (Cornwallis), Mahalwari (Mackenzie/Bird).
